readings.head: {{RunningHeader|unbending|6583|unbolt}}
readings.c1s1:
¶
'''unbending<sup>2</sup>''' (un-ben′ding), ''a.'' [< ''unbend'' + ''-ing''<sup>2</sup>.] Given up to relaxation or amusement.
{{smaller block|I hope it may entertain your lordship at an ''unbending'' hour.
{{right|''Rowe.''}}}}

'''unbendingly''' (un-ben′ding-li), ''adv.'' Without bending; obstinately.

'''unbendingness''' (un-ben′ding-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being unbending; inflexibility. ''Landor.''

'''unbeneficed''' (un-ben′ẹ̄-fist), ''a.'' Not enjoying or having a benefice. ''Dryden'', Hind and Panther, iii. 182.

'''unbeneficial''' (un-ben-ẹ̄-fish′al), ''a.'' Not beneficial; not advantageous, useful, profitable, or helpful. ''Milton.''

'''unbenefited''' (un-ben′ẹ̄-fit-ed), ''a.'' Having received no benefit, service, or advantage. ''V. Knox'', Liberal Education, App.

'''unbenighted''' (un-bẹ̄-nī′ted), ''a.'' Not benighted; never visited by darkness. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 682.

'''unbenign''' (un-bẹ̄-nīn′), ''a.'' Not benign; the reverse of benign; malignant. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 661.

'''unbenumb''' (un-bẹ̄-num′), ''v. t.'' To relieve from numbness; restore sensation to. ''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Handy-Crafts. [Rare.]

'''unbequothen†''', ''a.'' [ME. ''unbiquothen''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''bequothen'', obs. pp. of ''bequeath'', ''v.''] Not bequeathed.
{{smaller block|I wull that the residewe of the stuffe of myn houshold ''unbiquothen'' be divided equally betwen Edmund and William, my sones, and Anne, my daughter.
{{right|''Paston Letters'', III. 288.}}}}

'''unbereaven''' (un-bẹ̄-rē′vn), ''a.'' [An erroneous form, prop. ''unbereft''.] Not bereaved; unbe-
readings.c1s2:
reft. ''Mrs. Browning'', Child’s Grave at Florence. [Rare.]

'''unbereft''' (un-bẹ̄-reft′), ''a.'' Not bereaved or bereft. ''Sandys'', Æneid.

'''unbeseem''' (un-bẹ̄-sēm′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''beseem.''] Not to be fit for or worthy of; be unbecoming or not befitting to. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Ah! may’st thou ever be what now thou art,
Nor ''unbeseem'' the promise of thy spring.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', To Ianthe.}}}}

'''unbeseeming''' (un-bẹ̄-sē′ming), ''a.'' Unbecoming; not befitting; unsuitable.
{{smaller block|Was not that ''unbeseeming'' a King?
{{right|''N. Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, I. 427.}}}}

'''unbeseemingly''' (un-bẹ̄-sē′ming-li), ''adv.'' In an unbeseeming or unbecoming manner; unworthily. ''Barrow'', Works, III., ser. 6.

'''unbeseemingness''' (un-bẹ̄-sē′ming-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unbeseeming. ''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, Jeroboam’s Wife.

'''unbesought''' (un-bẹ̄-sôt′), ''a.'' Not besought; not sought by petition or entreaty. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 1058.

'''unbespeak''' (un-bẹ̄-spēk′), ''v. t.'' To revoke or put off, as something spoken for beforehand; annul, as an order, invitation, or engagement.
{{smaller block|Pretending that the corps stinks, they will bury it to night privately, and so will ''unbespeak'' all their guests.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, Oct. 30, 1661.}}}}
readings.c1s3:
¶
{{smaller block|I can immediately run back and ''unbespeak'' what I have order’d.
{{right|''Garrick'', Lying Valet, i.}}}}

'''unbestowed''' (un-bē-stōd′), ''a.'' Not bestowed; not given, granted, or conferred; not disposed of. ''Bacon'', Henry VII., p. 216.

'''unbethink†''' (un-bē-thingk′), ''v. t.'' Not to bethink. [Rare and erroneous.]
{{smaller block|The Lacedæmonian foot (a nation of all other the most obstinate in maintaining their ground) . . . ''unbethought'' themselves to disperse and retire.
{{right|''Cotton'', tr. of Montaigne’s Essays, xi. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unbetide''' (un-bẹ̄-tīd′), ''v. i.'' To fail to happen or betide.
{{smaller block|Thilke thing that God seth to bityde, it ne may nat ''unbityde.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 6.}}}}

'''unbettered''' (un-bet′ėrd), ''a.'' Not bettered or mitigated. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>From kings, and priests, and statesmen, war arose,
Whose safety is man’s deep ''unbettered'' woe.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Queen Mab, iv.}}}}

'''unbewares†''' (un-bẹ̄-wãrz′), ''adv.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''beware;'' erroneously for ''unawares.''] Unaware; unawares.
{{smaller block|To the intent that by their coming ''unbewares'' they might do the greater distruction.
{{right|''J. Brende'', tr. of Quintus Curtius, iv.}}}}

'''unbias''' (un-bī′a̤s), ''v. t.'' To free from bias; turn or free from prejudice or prepossession.
{{smaller block|The truest service a private man may hope to do his country is by ''unbiassing'' his mind as much as possible.
{{right|''Swift'', Sentiments of a Ch. of Eng. Man, i.}}}}

'''unbiased, unbiassed''' (un-bī′a̤st), ''a.'' Free from bias, undue partiality, or prejudice; impartial: as, an ''unbiased'' mind; an ''unbiased'' opinion or
readings.c2s1:
¶
{{smaller block|All men . . . lean to mercy when ''unbiassed'' by passions or interest.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, letter xxxviii.}}}}

'''unbiasedly, unbiassedly''' (un-bī′ast-li), ''adv.'' Without bias or prejudice; impartially. ''Locke'', Conduct of the Understanding, § 3.

'''unbiasedness, unbiassedness''' (un-bī′ast-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unbiased; freedom from bias or prejudice; impartiality.

'''unbid''' (un-bid′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not bid; unbidden.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thorns also and thistles it shall bring thee forth
''Unbid.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 204.}}}}
'''2†.''' Without having said prayers. ''Spenser'', F. Q., I. ix. 54.

'''unbidden''' (un-bid′n), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unbiden''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''bidden.''] '''1.''' Not bidden; not commanded; hence, spontaneous.—'''2.''' Uninvited; not requested to attend.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unbidden'' guests
Are often welcomest when they are gone.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., ii. 2. 55.}}}}

'''unbide†''' (un-bīd′), ''v. i.'' To go away; refuse to remain or stay. ''Testament of Love.''

'''unbind''' (un-bīnd′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unbound'', ppr. ''unbinding.'' [< ME. ''unbinden'', < AS. ''unbindan'' (= OFries. ''undbinda, onbinda'' = D. ''ontbinden'' = G. ''entbinden''); as ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bind''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To release from bands or restraint, as the hands or feet of a prisoner; free.
{{smaller block|Tak now my soule, ''unbind'' me of this unreste.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1339.}}
<poem>How myȝt god me of care ''vnbinde'',
Sithen god loueth trouthe so verrili?</poem>
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 97.}}}}
readings.c2s2:
'''2.''' To unfasten, as a band or tie.
{{smaller block|And death ''unbind'' my chain.
{{right|''Whittier'', Knight of St. John.}}}}

'''unbirdly''' (un-bėrd′li), ''adv.'' Unlike or unworthy of a bird. ''Cowley'', Of Liberty. [A nonce-word.]

'''unbishop''' (un-bish′up), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bishop.''] To deprive of episcopal orders; divest of the rank or office of bishop. ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.

'''unbitt''' (un-bit′), ''v. t.'' ''Naut.'', to remove the turns of from the bitts: as, to ''unbitt'' a cable.

'''unbitted''' (un-bit′ed), ''a.'' Unbridled; uncontrolled.
{{smaller block|Our carnal stings, our ''unbitted'' lusts.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 3. 335.}}}}

'''unbitten, unbit''' (un-bit′n, un-bit′), ''p. a.'' Not bitten.
{{smaller block|''Unbit'' by rage canine of dying rich.
{{right|''Young.''}}}}

'''unblamable''' (un-blā′ma̤-bl), ''a.'' Not blamable; not culpable; innocent. Also spelled ''unblameable.''
{{smaller block|To secure myself or the public against the future by positive inflictions upon the injurious . . . is also within the moderation of an ''unblamable'' defence.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 18, Pref.}}}}

'''unblamableness''' (un-blā′ma̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unblamable, or not chargeable with blame or fault. ''South.'' Also spelled ''unblameableness.''

'''unblamably''' (un-blā′ma̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unblamable manner; so as to incur no blame. 1 Thess. ii. 10. Also spelled ''unblameably.''

'''unblamed''' (un-blāmd′), ''a.'' Not blamed; free
readings.c2s3:
from censure; innocent.
{{smaller block|So . . . ''unblamed'' a life. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, ii. 4.}}}}

'''unbleached''' (un-blēcht′), ''a.'' Not bleached; of the color that it has after weaving: noting cloth.

'''unbleaching''' (un-blē′ching), ''a.'' Not bleaching; not becoming white or pale. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Blood’s ''unbleaching'' stain. {{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, i.}}}}

'''unbleeding''' (un-blē′ding), ''a.'' Not bleeding; not suffering loss of blood: as, “''unbleeding'' wounds,” ''Daniel'', To Sir T. Egerton. [Rare.]

'''unblemishable''' (un-blem′ish-ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being blemished. ''Milton.''

'''unblemished''' (un-blem′isht), ''a.'' Not blemished; not stained; free from turpitude, reproach, or deformity; pure; spotless: as, an ''unblemished'' reputation or life; an ''unblemished'' moral character.

'''unblenched†''' (un-blencht′), ''a.'' Not daunted or disconcerted; unconfounded. ''Milton'', Comus, l. 730.

'''unbless†''' (un-bles′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bless.''] To make unhappy; neglect to make happy.
{{smaller block|Thou dost beguile the world, ''unbless'' some mother. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, iii.}}}}

'''unblessed''' (un-blest′ or un-bles′ed), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unblessed'', ''onblissed''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''blessed.''] Same as ''unblest.''
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|Every inordinate cup is ''unblessed.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 3. 311.}}}}

'''unblessedness''' (un-bles′ed-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unblessed; wretchedness. ''Udall.''

'''unblest''' (un-blest′), ''a.'' [A later spelling of ''unblessed.''] Not blessed; excluded from benediction; hence, cursed; wretched; unhappy.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ill that He blesses is our good,
And ''unblest'' good is ill.</poem>
{{right|''F. W. Faber'', Hymns.}}}}

'''unblind''' (un-blīnd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''blind.''] To free from blindness; give sight to; open the eyes of. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It is not too late to ''unblind'' some of the people.
{{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, ii. 196. (''Davies.'')}}
Keep his vision clear from speck, his inward sight ''unblind.''
{{right|''Keats'', Birthplace of Burns.}}}}

'''unblissful''' (un-blis′fu̇l), ''a.'' Unhappy. ''Tennyson'', Dream of Fair Women.

'''unblithe''' (un-blīᴛ̵ʜ′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unblithe'', < AS. ''unblīthe'' (= OHG. ''unblīdi''); as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''blithe.''] Not blithe; not happy.

'''unblock''' (un-blok′), ''v. i.'' In ''whist'', to play an unnecessarily high card, in order to avoid interrupting a partner’s long suit.

'''unblooded''' (un-blud′ed), ''a.'' Not marked or distinguished by improved blood; not thoroughbred: as, an ''unblooded'' horse.

'''unbloodied''' (un-blud′id), ''a.'' Not made bloody. ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 193.

'''unbloody''' (un-blud′i), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not stained with blood.
{{smaller block|<poem>This hath brought</poem>}}
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>That bold, bad man, . . . pretending still,
With hard ''unblushing'' front, the public good.</poem>
{{right|''T. Edwards'', Sonnets, xiv.}}}}

'''unblushingly''' (un-blush′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unblushing or shameless manner.

'''unboastful''' (un-bōst′fụl), ''a.'' Not boasting; unassuming; modest. ''Thomson'', Summer.

'''unbodied''' (un-bod′id), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no material body; incorporeal.
{{smaller block|<poem>He ’s such an airy, thin, ''unbodied'' coward,
That no revenge can catch him.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, v. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Freed from the body; disembodied.
{{smaller block|Like an ''unbodied'' joy whose race is just begun.
{{right|''Shelley'', To a Skylark, iii.}}}}

'''unboding''' (un-bō′ding), ''a.'' Not anticipating; not looking for.
{{smaller block|<poem>I grow in worth, and wit, and sense,
''Unboding'' critic-pen.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Will Waterproof, vi.}}}}

'''unbodkined''' (un-bod′kind), ''a.'' Unfastened with a bodkin; freed from fastening by a bodkin. ''Mrs. Browning'', Duchess May. [Rare.]

'''unbody†''' (un-bod′i), ''v. i.'' To be deprived of the body; become disembodied.
{{smaller block|The fate wolde his soule sholde ''unbodye.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 1550.}}}}

'''unbolt''' (un-bōlt′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bolt''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To release or allow to be opened by withdrawing a bolt: as, to ''unbolt'' a door.
{{smaller block|He shall ''unbolt'' the gates. {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iv. 2. 3.}}}}
